name: Adam Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a stamping press at a metal plant that makes panels and brackets for washing machines and dryers. A coil of steel feeds in one end, the press comes down at about four hundred tonnes, and out come side panels, forty a minute. I watch the feed, change the coils with the crane, check parts against the gauge and keep my hands well away from the die. I'm a year and a half in and still not allowed to do die changes on my own, Kev the setter does those and I hand him the bolts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the job like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's honest work and it pays well, the shift premium got me the deposit on a little terraced house with some help from my dad. I'm also a volunteer firefighter on call two nights a week, so I like work where you know what you're doing and do it properly. I use AI now and then, my mate showed me how to ask it about the fire service exams. The worst bit is the noise, ear defenders all day, and the ache in your back from leaning over the gauge table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, people still need people. I wouldn't post anything, but at work we'd have a laugh about all the experts who said otherwise. My dad would say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd suit me fine. I'd keep learning the press, maybe do a proper maintenance apprenticeship in a couple of years, and pay off the house. Nothing about it worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep overpaying the mortgage by about two hundred a month and ask the plant about their maintenance apprenticeship scheme next intake. I'd keep doing the fire service on the side. Same life, just a bit more settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship rather than a college course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you learn from someone who's done it, on the real machines, and you get paid while you learn. That's how my dad learned plumbing and how Kev learned setting. College is fine for some, but I'd rather learn with a spanner in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your girlfriend Ruth feel about the house and the plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a dental nurse, she's very sensible, she'd say keep overpaying and stop buying power tools. We're not married yet, but we're talking about it for next year. She likes that I've got a trade in sight.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, people still need people. He wouldn't post, but they'd laugh at the experts at work, and his dad would say he told him so.
S0.think: It'd suit him fine: keep learning the press, do a maintenance apprenticeship in a couple of years and pay off the house. Nothing worries him.
S0.do: Keeps overpaying the mortgage by about two hundred a month and applies to the plant's next maintenance apprenticeship intake. Continues as an on-call volunteer firefighter.
S0.quote: College is fine for some, but I'd rather learn with a spanner in my hand.
S0.fieldNote: His values centre on learning a trade on the job, from people who've done it. Owning a small house already gives him a sense of being settled. The volunteer fire service is a big part of who he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have every right to bring in new machines, that's how they stay in business. Workers just need to keep up. I'd say the answer is more apprenticeships, not more handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bit of the job, feeding coils and checking parts, could be done by a robot arm and a camera, I know that. But someone has to maintain the robots, and if I get on the apprenticeship I'd be that someone. I'd want to see it working at another plant first, then I'd go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep an eye on the big appliance plant on the bypass, because if they automate, we'll follow. Once it's proven, I'd push hard for the maintenance apprenticeship, even if it means a pay cut for a year. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage so I'm safe either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a push to get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take a pay cut for a year. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with my savings, about eight months' worth, and the house payments being low. It'd mean no holiday and fewer takeaways, but it's worth it for a trade. My dad did the same when he started out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plant would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, funnily enough, even though he's the expert. He's fifty and he hates computers, and the new presses are all touchscreens. I'd help him if he let me, but he's proud.

S1.say: I'd say companies have every right to bring in new machines to stay in business and workers need to keep up. The answer is more apprenticeships, not handouts.
S1.think: He knows coil feeding and part checks suit a robot arm and camera. Someone still has to maintain robots, and he'd aim to be that person once he's seen it work elsewhere.
S1.do: Watches the appliance plant on the bypass, then pushes for the maintenance apprenticeship once automation is proven, accepting a year's pay cut. Keeps overpaying the mortgage.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a push to get on with things.
S1.quote: He's fifty and he hates computers, and the new presses are all touchscreens.
S1.fieldNote: He accepts companies' right to automate without resentment, consistent with his free-market views. His steady style shows in waiting for the bypass plant to go first. A pay cut for a trade feels natural to him because his father did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to cope with. The worry is the government will use it as an excuse to put everyone on handouts instead of helping people work. I'd say we need to keep people doing real jobs, whatever that takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the robots maintain the robots, so the apprenticeship plan's gone. I've got a house and a mortgage, smaller than most, but still a mortgage. I'd be thinking a lot about what's left that people still want from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw every spare penny at the mortgage to get it as small as possible, and cut takeaways and gadgets to nothing. I'd keep the press job till the end, and ask the fire service about full-time roles, because I'd guess people want a person carrying them out of a burning house. I'd lean on my dad and Ruth's family if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be worried most of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want a person carrying them out of a fire. Are you sure that holds with robots that can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. Maybe a robot could do it better, it wouldn't breathe smoke. But I think people would still want a face at the door, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like handouts. If the government offered a basic income, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, but I'd keep doing something useful too, the fire service, helping my dad. I wouldn't want to sit at home on it. That's not how I was raised.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast to cope with and fear the government will use it as an excuse for handouts instead of helping people work. We need to keep people in real jobs.
S2.think: With robots maintaining robots in two years, his apprenticeship plan is gone. He has a small mortgage and wonders what work people will still want from people.
S2.do: Pours every spare penny into the mortgage and cuts takeaways and gadgets. Keeps the press job to the end, asks about full-time firefighting roles, and leans on his and Ruth's families if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed and worried most of the time.
S2.quote: Maybe a robot could do it better, it wouldn't breathe smoke. But I think people would still want a face at the door, at least for a while.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture kills his trade plan, which is the source of his calm elsewhere. He'd accept a basic income only alongside useful work, in line with how he was raised. Firefighting is his instinctive refuge, though he admits it might not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but people can still do something with it. Learn a trade that needs a person, pay off your debts, look after your family. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a couple of years on the apprenticeship and some on the tools before the end. That's something, even if it's not a whole career. I'd want to watch what happens at the big plants first and see if maintenance really lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship starting next intake, and keep overpaying the house, aiming to clear it by thirty-two if I can. Ruth and I would probably bring the wedding forward and keep it small. I'd use AI tools to help me study, my mate says it's good for the theory bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's on my mind, but I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want us settled, married and in the house, before things change. A big do costs money we might need. Small wedding, church, family, a meal at the pub, that's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd wait to see if maintenance lasts. With five years, would you still wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe, but not longer. With two years there's no time, with ten I could wait, five's in between. I'd start the apprenticeship anyway, because it's useful even if it doesn't last forever.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but usable: learn a trade that needs a person, pay off debts and look after your family. That's what he'd say at work.
S3.think: Five years gives him a couple of years on the apprenticeship and a few on the tools before the end. He'd watch big plants to see if maintenance work really lasts.
S3.do: Starts the apprenticeship at the next intake and overpays the mortgage to clear it by thirty-two. Brings the wedding with Ruth forward and keeps it small, using AI tools to study theory.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: Small wedding, church, family, a meal at the pub, that's plenty.
S3.fieldNote: He thinks out loud about how waiting time scales with the timeline, which shows his steady approach adapting. Marriage and a paid-off house are his idea of being safe. AI comes in only as a study aid, recommended by a friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, so there's no excuse not to get ready. Learn a trade, pay your way, look after your own. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships and family businesses, not just pay people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means a proper trade, maybe even a small business of my own fixing machines for farms and workshops. I'd be thirty-seven, house paid, probably kids. It ends anyway, but I'd have had a good run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, qualify in about four years, then maybe go self-employed around year six. I'd keep paying down the house so it's clear by the time it hits. I'd keep the fire service going because it's the thing I'd most want to keep doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I think I'd cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Self-employed fixing machines. Why that and not staying at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a small business is yours, nobody can automate you out of a job except yourself. Farmers round here have old equipment that needs someone who knows it. And my dad ran his own plumbing business, so I've seen it done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about all this, if you had them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to do something useful with their hands and their heads. And that work isn't just for money, it's how you look after people. Whatever the robots do, I'd want them to know that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair time, so there's no excuse not to get ready. Government should back apprenticeships and family businesses, not pay people to sit at home.
S4.think: Ten years means a proper trade, maybe his own business fixing farm and workshop machines, a paid-off house and children by thirty-seven. It ends anyway, but he'd have had a good run.
S4.do: Completes the four-year apprenticeship and considers going self-employed around year six. Keeps paying down the house to clear it before AGI and keeps volunteering with the fire service.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, confident he'd cope.
S4.quote: Because a small business is yours, nobody can automate you out of a job except yourself.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, his traditional values and steady pace fit together: trade first, then his own business, as his father did. He sees work as a way of looking after people. The fire service is what he'd fight hardest to keep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan is a trade, and you can't learn a trade in two years when the trade's disappearing. What would help is the government paying for apprenticeships in whatever still needs people, and help for family businesses to keep people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the fire service. That's the bit of my life I'd fight hardest to keep, and I think a lot of people have something like it, a team or a club or a church. If work goes, those things matter more, not less.

headlineQuote: If work goes, those things matter more, not less.
portrait: Adam Abbott is a 27-year-old junior stamping press operator at a plant making washing machine panels, still handing bolts to the setter during die changes. He owns a small terraced house bought with help from his father, has about eight months saved, and volunteers as an on-call firefighter. Traditional and pro-business, he believes in apprenticeships over handouts and uses AI now and then. He's calm with a plateau or steady change, planning a maintenance apprenticeship once he's seen others automate. AGI in two years alarms him because it kills his trade plan, while five or ten years let him train, marry Ruth and pay off the house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to learn a trade when the trade itself is disappearing.
whatWouldHelp: Government-funded apprenticeships in work that still needs people, and support for family businesses to keep staff on.
